review.decision_reason: sas-temper is a standalone, installable scientific package for small-angle X-ray/neutron scattering fits and automated reproducibility analysis. I inspected its public ORNL source tree, actual BSD-3-Clause grant, package setup, versioned tags, examples, tests, and available manuals. The DOE software record associates the exact code with ORNL and DOE Office of Science scientific user-facilities funding. Its SoftwareX paper documents the exact tool, command-line/configuration workflow and reusable model-fitting methods; a later 2023 research article explicitly reports using sas-temper to fit SANS data. Version 0.4.0 was tagged in March 2025, so the current-use/freshness check is met. The first defensible licensed-source year is 2020: the full grant was added in the v0.1.0 release commit on 2020-10-08.

government_provenance.note: The official DOE software record identifies this exact sas-temper software, its ORNL authors/recipient, and DOE Office of Science Basic Energy Sciences Scientific User Facilities funding. The source license names UT-Battelle, LLC; ORNL’s official software profile also classifies sas-temper as an ORNL software output.

public_source.note: The canonical ORNL GitLab repository is public. Anonymous API inspection exposed the current Python package source, setup.py, requirements, examples, tests, documentation files, and README without credentials.

eligible_license.note: Inspected the full current LICENSE: standard OSI-approved BSD 3-Clause terms, copyright UT-Battelle, LLC. GitLab history shows the initial full grant in commit 8f52fcf0c335bbe38c234482dae01cec1cf6106e on 2020-10-08, the same commit used for the v0.1.0 tag; that release contains the functional package.

primary_evidence.note: The SoftwareX article is specifically about sas-temper and documents fitting workflows, YAML inputs, unattended execution, the manual, and integration into facility workflows. The later 2023 paper at https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4125/3/1/9 explicitly says its SANS data fitting used sas-temper. The official ORNL software page records this exact product as software.

review.decision_reason: The FY17 USGS report documents this script as one component of a historical photo-publishing toolkit and gives it a useful Adobe Bridge installation guide, but the assigned repository is not the separate web-map application and has no versioned release, current product-specific use/support, or demonstrated independent reuse. The repository is explicitly archival, and the primary-evidence/notability baseline is not met. In addition, the source file attributes underlying DIYMetadata code to Paul Riggott while the repo offers CC0 without an upstream grant for that original code; its eligible-license scope remains unresolved. The primary-evidence failure is independently decisive for rejection.

government_provenance.note: The official FY17 CDI funded-project report identifies Sarah Nagorsen (USGS) as PI, describes the photo-publishing toolkit, and links this exact photometadata repository as its Adobe Bridge EXIF script.

public_source.note: The public USGS GitLab project exposes the GeotagPhotoMetadata.jsx script and CSV template without credentials.

eligible_license.note: Root LICENSE.md claims a worldwide CC0 dedication for the project, but the actual script header says DIYMetadata was written by Paul Riggott and modified/renamed by USGS author Sarah Nagorsen. No grant covering Riggott's original code was located, so CC0 scope for this material derivative cannot be verified.

primary_evidence.note: The report supports historical inclusion of the script in one Grand Canyon photo collection workflow, not a current standalone product or independent reuse. The assigned repository is marked Archival, has no tags/versioned release, and is distinct from the separate JavaScript/Python web-map application; no current-use/support signal or notability pathway for this exact script repo was found.

review.product_identity: GeotagPhotoMetadata.jsx, a batch Adobe Bridge script for inserting CSV/tab-delimited photo metadata into image XMP/EXIF fields; one component of a separate Grand Canyon photo web-map toolkit
review.agency: U.S. Geological Survey, Community for Data Integration FY17 project; principal investigator Sarah Nagorsen (USGS)
review.geography: Grand Canyon region, Arizona, United States; historical geologic field-photo collection publishing workflow
review.license: Repository claims CC0-1.0 worldwide, but the scope over upstream DIYMetadata code by Paul Riggott is unresolved
review.status_note: The script identifies Riggott as the original DIYMetadata author and dates Nagorsen's modification to 2017-08-15; the file appears in the public project tree by 2017-10-16. The project-wide LICENSE.md was added 2020-03-23, which is not a defensible first open-source year while the upstream license scope remains unclear. README documentation requires Adobe Bridge CS6 or CC; code.json now marks this project Archival, and its 2024 metadataLastUpdated field is not a source change.

titles: Code for Value Decomposition Graph Network and environment for AMR on linear advection

source_rows.metadata_screen_reason: DOE CODE reports a named license claim; this is a discovery screen only and does not establish an OSI-approved or source-confirmed license.

review.decision_reason: MARL-AMR is a distinct LLNL scientific research implementation of Value Decomposition Graph Network (VDGN) and a multi-agent environment for linear-advection adaptive-mesh-refinement experiments. The assigned personal-account URL redirects to the current LLNL GitHub repository; I inspected the canonical public source, complete BSD-3-Clause LICENSE, LLNL/DOE NOTICE, setup/install script, and training/testing instructions. Its exact implementation is the subject of the peer-reviewed AAMAS 2023 paper, and the repository provides user instructions and a pretrained model. The first defensible public licensed-source year is 2023: the canonical repository’s initial source commit and 2023 license are dated 2023-08-15.

government_provenance.note: The current repository NOTICE states this specific work was produced under the auspices of DOE by Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory under contract DE-AC52-07NA27344. The README bears LLNL-CODE-853184 and the AAMAS paper identifies multiple authors as LLNL researchers.

public_source.note: The assigned https://github.com/011235813/marl-amr URL redirects to the public LLNL-owned canonical repo at github.com/llnl/marl-amr. The current tree exposes source, install.sh, setup.py, requirements, pretrained results, and evaluation scripts without credentials.

eligible_license.note: Inspected the complete current standard BSD 3-Clause grant, copyright 2023 Lawrence Livermore National Security, LLC and contributors. The README states SPDX BSD-3 and links this LICENSE and the DOE NOTICE; no embedded conflicting product-code license was found.

primary_evidence.note: The official AAMAS proceedings contain the exact peer-reviewed MARL-AMR/VDGN paper and identify LLNL authors. The repository README explicitly identifies this tree as the code for that paper and documents setup, training, testing, and a pretrained policy.

review.product_identity: MARL-AMR, the standalone Python implementation of VDGN and a multi-agent linear-advection environment for adaptive mesh refinement; not a general-purpose AMR solver
review.agency: Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, U.S. Department of Energy
review.license: BSD-3-Clause
review.status_note: The DOE lead is a redirect/migration alias; GitHub resolves it to llnl/marl-amr. The canonical repository contains one initial commit c6248f8 (2023-08-15) with substantive project files and BSD-3 LICENSE. The subsequent upstream paper is exactly about this implementation and appears in the official AAMAS 2023 proceedings.

source_rows.metadata_screen_reason: DOE CODE reports a named license claim; this is a discovery screen only and does not establish an OSI-approved or source-confirmed license.

review.decision_reason: SEPT is an LLNL research implementation associated with a peer-reviewed ICLR 2020 paper, public code, and a complete BSD-3-Clause grant. The root README contains experiment setup and train/test instructions; however, the last source push is 2022-06-13, more than four years before this review, and I found no post-2022 product-specific support, release, or use. The repository also bundles the separately MIT-licensed hip-mdp-public environment subtree, which must not be mistaken as covered by the root BSD grant. Hold for a current-use signal and product-level source scope clarification.

government_provenance.note: The repository’s NOTICE says this work was produced by LLNL under U.S. DOE contract DE-AC52-07NA27344. The exact ICLR paper’s authors include LLNL researchers; no account-name-only inference is used.

public_source.note: The assigned public GitHub repository and code are accessible without credentials, including algorithm source, experiment configs, results, and instructions.

eligible_license.note: Inspected the full current root BSD 3-Clause LICENSE, copyright 2020 Lawrence Livermore National Security, LLC. The bundled hip-mdp-public subtree is separately documented as MIT-licensed in its own README; this is a separate license scope and is not represented as covered by the root BSD file.

primary_evidence.note: The LLNL-hosted paper identifies the exact SEPT algorithm and ICLR 2020 publication; the root README links this repo to the paper and gives experimental workflows. But last push was 2022-06-13 and no post-2022 deployment, independent reuse, support, or current distribution was found. The old paper alone does not meet the baseline’s current-use exception.

review.product_identity: Single Episode Policy Transfer (SEPT), an experimental reinforcement-learning implementation for adapting policies to unknown environment dynamics in one test episode; includes a separately MIT-licensed HiP-MDP benchmark subtree
review.agency: Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, U.S. Department of Energy
review.license: BSD-3-Clause
review.status_note: GitHub identifies 2020-02-12 as the initial open-source commit with the root LICENSE; the repository was last pushed 2022-06-13. README documents hip-mdp-public as code from the 2017 Killian et al. work and links the separate MIT source repository; preserve this embedded third-party license boundary.

review.decision_reason: Surface Method Raytracer is a substantive LLNL/DOE research code with a full MIT grant for Lawrence Livermore National Security-owned files, a v1.0 README with run/test guidance, and a matching 2024 peer-reviewed paper on its surface method. However, the current tree embeds at least three specifically credited third-party MATLAB routines: `lglnodes.m` and `lgwt.m` by Greg von Winckel and `GenerateCentralDiffsCoefs.m` by Manuel A. Diaz. The first two original MathWorks File Exchange records have BSD-2 terms, but those embedded copies omit the required copyright/license notices; no authoritative grant for the Diaz routine was verified. Hold until the rights and license scope of all shipped code are resolved; do not label the entire tree MIT.

government_provenance.note: The first-party NOTICE says the work was produced under DOE auspices by Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory under contract DE-AC52-07NA27344. The README names the LLNL code-release number LLNL-CODE-862911, and the actual root grant assigns copyright to Lawrence Livermore National Security, LLC.

public_source.note: The assigned lower-case repository URL resolves case-insensitively to this public GitHub repository. Its MATLAB source, problem configurations, examples, tests, README, NOTICE, and LICENSE are viewable without credentials.

eligible_license.note: The inspected root LICENSE.txt is the complete MIT grant for Lawrence Livermore National Security, LLC. But the same shipped tree includes Greg von Winckel’s `lgwt` and `lglnodes` routines; the original MathWorks File Exchange records expose BSD-2 grants (https://www.mathworks.com/matlabcentral/fileexchange/4540-legendre-gauss-quadrature-weights-and-nodes and https://www.mathworks.com/matlabcentral/fileexchange/4775-legende-gauss-lobatto-nodes-and-weights), while the copied files omit their required BSD notice text. The file by Manuel A. Diaz is also credited but carries no per-file grant, and its authoritative license scope was not verified. The aggregate license is therefore unresolved.

primary_evidence.note: The peer-reviewed Journal of Computational Physics article describes the same conservative Surface Method for first-collision source treatment, names Alex B. Christensen, and presents numerical tests. The repository README identifies Surface Method Raytracer v1.0, LLNL-CODE-862911, explains the interior-point and surface methods, gives MATLAB run instructions, and includes example problems and comparisons—supporting a named scientific code product, not an unverified claim of separate deployment.

The public repository contains the full MIT-licensed Python package, tests, usage/installation documentation, and CLI; PyPI lists current version 0.8.5 from May 2026. The first grant and first substantive parser implementation are both dated 2018-11-29. Attribution is to Turing-developed software within the publicly supported AIDA project, not to a government-authored package.

government_provenance.note: The official AIDA report lists CleverCSV by exact name and repository as one of AIDA's software outputs, and states the project received UK Government Defence & Security Programme funding in support of the Turing (Apr 2017–Mar 2019) and Turing support under EPSRC grant EP/N510129/1 (Apr 2019–May 2021). The Turing AIDA page separately describes CleverCSV and links its exact repository and paper: https://www.turing.ac.uk/research/research-projects/artificial-intelligence-data-analytics-aida/why-practical-data-analytics-still-so-painfuland-how-we-can-help. This supports an AIDA project-funding relationship; it does not make the Turing a public body or imply that government authored the package.

public_source.note: The assigned public repository exposes package source, tests, documentation, packaging files, and the root license without credentials. Its README links to PyPI, ReadTheDocs, an interactive Binder demo, and usage examples; PyPI lists version 0.8.5 uploaded 2026-05-11.

eligible_license.note: The current root LICENSE contains the complete standard MIT grant and names The Alan Turing Institute. License history shows it was added in initial commit e957ce46a71a52e976a323978f02352a985933c4 on 2018-11-29 at 13:44:33 UTC. The first substantive parser implementation was added two minutes later in commit 47853db9737475343ea885de395afe48b6b98029, so the first defensible public licensed-code year is 2018.

primary_evidence.note: The README documents install via pip, a library API and CLI, examples, API/docs links, and cites the peer-reviewed 2019 paper on the exact dialect-detection method. Turing's AIDA page names the package and links its code and related publication; the AIDA final report lists it as a software output. This is a research-software/scientific-use pathway, not a claim of public-service deployment.

review.decision_reason: OpenStad headless is a mature, widely used open-source municipal participation platform with official government evidence and deployment guidance, but the whole monorepo's license scope is inconsistent in current first-party records. The root LICENSE.md and package manifests say MIT, publiccode.yml says ISC, and some bundled widget CSS carries EUPL-1.2 notices. Hold until the maintainers clarify whether those files are retained third-party/legacy works or included in the current platform-wide grant.

government_provenance.note: The manifest names Gemeente Amsterdam as organization and lists multiple participating municipalities/provinces as funders and users; the official IPLO government page says Amsterdam and other municipalities developed/offered the open-source platform.

public_source.note: The canonical public headless monorepo exposes API, CMS, authentication/image services, widgets, deployment charts, and installation documentation without credentials.

eligible_license.note: The root license text is MIT, but current publiccode.yml says ISC and bundled widget CSS contains EUPL-1.2 file-level notices; the effective grant for the complete application family is not unambiguous from reviewed materials.

primary_evidence.note: The Dutch government's IPLO page describes OpenStad as an open-source municipal participation platform developed by Amsterdam with other municipalities; official OpenStad documentation and website provide setup, deployment, and administrator guidance and report use by many public organizations.

review.product_identity: OpenStad headless: municipal digital-participation platform monorepo
review.agency: Municipality of Amsterdam (originating public sponsor), with participating Dutch municipalities and provinces
review.license: Unresolved for the complete monorepo: root LICENSE.md states MIT (Gemeente Amsterdam); publiccode.yml says ISC; some widget CSS retains EUPL-1.2 notices; dependencies and bundled assets may carry separate licenses
review.family_note: The assigned Amsterdam repository URL is now represented by the `openstad/openstad-headless` canonical repo per its current publiccode URL. Treat this as one current headless platform monorepo; do not split its apps/packages into separate products or merge the older legacy OpenStad codebase without separate review.
review.status_note: First root LICENSE.md was MIT in commit https://github.com/openstad/openstad-headless/commit/cd458bb80b34774149ac074d0e46d2017553d208 (2020-03-27); a new root MIT grant was added in 2025 and LICENSE renamed/updated at https://github.com/openstad/openstad-headless/commit/575730185860b3d2f9cd8169c90270ed823c1e12. Current publiccode.yml still says ISC and source CSS includes EUPL-1.2 notices, so record 2020 as first licensed-source year but hold the present whole-product license claim for clarification.

review.decision_reason: Amsterdam/signals is the public Django backend/API and case-management codebase for Signalen. The official Dutch OSS Register identifies Signalen as an Amsterdam initiative and reports its municipal production scale; Amsterdam's current city service page provides live operational evidence. The backend's own MPL-2.0 grant and 2018 first license-bearing commit are verified. Treat this as one Signalen product family with the separately reviewed frontend, not as a separate product for every fork/component.

government_provenance.note: The official Dutch OSS Register identifies Gemeente Amsterdam as the owner of the Signalen project, says it was developed at Amsterdam's initiative, and links the canonical Amsterdam frontend. Amsterdam/signals' README identifies that frontend as its associated web interface; its application-design docs say the backend was developed for and by the municipality.

public_source.note: The public repository contains the Django application/API, tests, Docker Compose development/deployment configuration, and technical docs; source is readable without credentials. Its docs identify the separately maintained browser frontend.

eligible_license.note: Inspected the actual LICENSE text: Mozilla Public License 2.0. Git history shows the first LICENSE-bearing commit on 2018-06-06: https://github.com/Amsterdam/signals/commit/8167a338f399b371b3680b8caee47b2b431467f1. This determines the grant for this repository only, not every linked Signalen stack component.

primary_evidence.note: The official register's Signalen entry reports approximately 300,000 annual Amsterdam public-space reports and more than 1,400 municipal staff working with the system, and says the open-source software can be used by other governments. Amsterdam's city page links the live resident reporting service: https://www.amsterdam.nl/leefomgeving/een-melding-doen/.

review.product_identity: Signalen municipal reporting and case-management system (this repository supplies the Django backend/API)
review.agency: Municipality of Amsterdam (Gemeente Amsterdam; project origin and steward)
review.license: MPL-2.0 (Amsterdam/signals backend repository only; not a blanket license claim for linked components)
review.family_note: Treat Signalen as one product family with the separately reviewed Signalen/frontend web application. GitHub labels Signalen/backend as a fork of Amsterdam/signals, so it is not a distinct backend product. Other auxiliary repositories (including deployment charts/classification/mapserver) are separate codebases and are not licensed by this repository's LICENSE; do not infer their license scope from this review.
review.status_note: This repository is the backend/API, not the citizen-facing frontend. The official register and live city service establish product use; the first defensible public licensed-source year is 2018 based on the LICENSE-bearing commit dated 2018-06-06.

review.decision_reason: The assigned repository is the legacy CodeIgniter 3 PHP framework, not CodeIgniter 4. Although CodeIgniter originated at private vendor EllisLab, the official project history says it was acquired and stewarded by the British Columbia Institute of Technology (BCIT) beginning in 2014; the Province of British Columbia classifies BCIT as a public post-secondary institution authorized under provincial legislation. CodeIgniter 3.0 was released under MIT during that stewardship in 2015, with versioned releases and official installation/user guidance. The current project README describes CI3 as a legacy line receiving mostly security maintenance, so it is a maintained legacy product rather than the current mainline. No catalog entry added.

government_provenance.note: The official CodeIgniter credits state that the project was acquired by BCIT in 2014 and became community-maintained; the 2014 project-lead announcement details BCIT hosting the site/forum, transfer of GitHub/social accounts, and project-lead time. BCIT is listed by the Province as a public post-secondary institution authorized under provincial legislation: https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/education-training/post-secondary-education/find-a-program-or-institution/find-an-institution. I count its documented project stewardship during the CodeIgniter 3 release period as public-institution provenance, not as the original private EllisLab creation.

public_source.note: The assigned public repository explicitly identifies itself as the legacy CodeIgniter 3 source and links official user, installation, and release guidance. The CodeIgniter 4 successor is a separate product/repository and is not used to transfer claims to this CI3 row.

eligible_license.note: The repository's actual root license.txt grants the standard OSI-approved MIT License to the Software. The official CI3 changelog says version 3.0.0, released March 30, 2015, was relicensed from its prior proprietary terms to MIT; this establishes the eligible grant and its source line, while separately licensed dependencies retain their own notices.

primary_evidence.note: This agency-stewarded reusable framework has versioned releases (official changelog lists CI3.1.13, released March 3, 2022) and first-party download, installation, and user-guide documentation. The official repository says CI3 is in maintenance and receives mostly security updates; this is an agency-published software/release-and-guidance notability pathway, not a popularity-only case.

review.decision_reason: Leezenflow is a specific municipal green-wave assistant for cyclists, not merely a vendor product deployed by government: the City of Münster adopted the hackathon idea, built and evaluated a prototype using a Federal Ministry of Transport grant, later expanded the solution through the federal Model Projects Smart Cities program, and contracted bCyber GmbH to program and manufacture the devices. The exact assigned repository is the publicly accessible Python application code identified by the federal Smart City Dialog page, and its README plus LICENSE.txt grant GPL-3.0-or-later. The first public repository commit is dated 2022-01-31 and is titled “public release”; this source year is distinct from the 2019 hackathon idea and May 2021 first on-street test. Current official evidence describes ten installed devices and replication by CityLAB Berlin. No catalog entry added.

government_provenance.note: The federal Smart City Dialog page says Münster's city administration picked up the Münsterhack 2019 idea and implemented a prototype with a grant from the Federal Ministry of Transport and Digital Infrastructure; the municipal Smart City office coordinates it, and bCyber programmed/manufactured the devices. The city later expanded it under the Federal Model Projects Smart Cities program. This is government-funded/commissioned product development, not just public-sector use.

public_source.note: The federal source identifies this exact GitHub repository as the Python code for Leezenflow's traffic-signal phase reading, green-phase arrival prediction, and LED-display behavior. The public repository contains the application, tests, requirements, and setup/production instructions. eligible_license.note: The repository README states that this program is licensed under the GNU General Public License version 3 or, at the recipient's option, any later version; the root LICENSE.txt contains the complete GPLv3 text. This grant covers the first-party Python Leezenflow code in this repository; separately linked hardware documentation and third-party libraries have their own terms.

primary_evidence.note: The federal platform's 2025 product-specific page describes the operating municipal system, its ten-device installation in Münster, nine additional sites, user-facing cycling guidance, and ongoing support through the regular traffic-light operation. It also says CityLAB Berlin reused the solution as Kottiflow. This establishes documented operational deployment and independent reuse, not merely a code release or star count.

Although it implements the Italian PEC technical rules and is versioned/distributed through Maven Central with API/use documentation, no government creation, commissioning, funding or stewardship of this library was established; the Italian standard is the target, not provenance. No exact catalog match found; no catalog entry added.

Its link to Italian PEC technical regulations shows the software parses a government-defined format, not that an agency created, commissioned, funded or stewarded this parser. The inventory record is a discovery lead, not provenance.

public_source.note: The public canonical repository contains the Java parser library source, tests, build configuration, documentation and release history. It is distributed as the `app.tozzi:pec-parser` package, not just a source listing.

eligible_license.note: The actual root LICENSE is the complete Apache License 2.0, an OSI-approved grant for the library's first-party source; runtime dependencies have their own license terms. The root license was already present before the first library implementation code.

primary_evidence.note: Maven Central distributes the versioned `app.tozzi:pec-parser` library, and the official Developers Italia project detail records stable version 6.0.0, Maven/Gradle installation coordinates, API methods and PEC parsing guidance. No use evidence is inferred from its catalog listing.

public_source.note: This is the canonical, public, actively maintained multi-component server/client source repository. Current default-branch history is active in 2026 and the README links installation, architecture, API and developer documentation.

eligible_license.note: The current root LICENSE is the complete GNU Lesser General Public License v3.0 (LGPL-3.0), an OSI-approved grant for BigBlueButton-developed code. The full public source, exact dual-license scope, earliest public grant and substantial independent integration into Microsoft VS Code were checked separately. public_source.note: This is the actual public Rust command-line tool source, with tests, build instructions, user guide, release binaries and changelog; it is active and publicly downloadable.

primary_evidence.note: Microsoft's first-party vscode-ripgrep repository explicitly states that the package is used by VS Code and packages upstream ripgrep binaries; Microsoft VS Code's own search documentation likewise says workspace text search uses ripgrep. This is documented independent software reuse. Current ripgrep docs and releases support a usable distribution.

The public repository and license history date to 2016, but this source has no substantive commit after 2016 and the current CEOS deployments do not establish that they still run this v2 code rather than the later Open Data Cube implementations. Hold pending source-to-current-product parity or explicit archival-significance evidence.

government_provenance.note: NASA's official LAR-18928-1 record describes CEOS Data Cube Platform v2 as an open-source remote-sensing platform; CEOS records NASA among contributing agencies to its collaborative data-cube technology work (https://deliverables.ceos.org/task_manager/deliverables/522/).

public_source.note: The public repository contains the CEOS2 platform source, project files, and documentation; its latest commit is 2016-11-04.

eligible_license.note: The actual LICENSE grants Apache-2.0, and it was included in the first public repository commit dated 2016-07-20 (https://github.com/ceos-seo/Data_Cube_v2/commit/571d98f4a71157d7d2ce26dfec08378aa4072b6e).

primary_evidence.note: NASA's NTRS record describes the CEOS Data Cube Portal as open-source software for ingesting, processing, visualizing, and distributing analysis-ready remote-sensing data and cites NASA LaRC co-author Brian Killough.

review.geography: United States federal agency; international CEOS collaboration/deployments
review.license: Apache-2.0

review.decision_reason: Ceph is an open-source distributed storage product that began as a UCSC research system under product-specific funding from the U.S. Department of Energy/NNSA Advanced Simulation and Computing program and national laboratories. The assigned organization URL resolves to a multi-repository org; I scoped this review to the core ceph/ceph distribution and recorded its per-file licensing exceptions. Current releases, installation docs, and Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre's production 11PB/27PB clusters establish a significant maintained product. No exact catalog duplicate found; no catalog entry added.

government_provenance.note: The UCSC Storage Systems Research Center page describes its Ceph prototype/source and lists Department of Energy/NNSA, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, Los Alamos National Laboratory, Sandia National Laboratories, and NSF among project sponsors. The Ceph Foundation history independently states that Ceph began in a national-laboratory-funded effort; this is product-origin funding, not merely later government use.

public_source.note: The assigned https://github.com/ceph URL is an organization with many independent repositories; the canonical core distributed-storage product source is github.com/ceph/ceph. It is public and active, with build and test material and versioned release history. Review does not automatically include Ceph CSI, Rook, or other sibling projects.

eligible_license.note: The core source README states that most Ceph code is distributed under LGPL 2.1 or LGPL 3.0; COPYING enumerates file-specific terms. These are OSI-approved LGPL grants. Some headers/code use GPL, BSD-style or public-domain terms, and docs use CC BY-SA-3.0; the SILL's single LGPL-2.1-only claim is too narrow and is not treated as a uniform grant over every file.

primary_evidence.note: A Ceph case study coauthored by Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre staff documents two production Ceph clusters: 11 PB for general research and 27 PB for radio astronomy. Current 2026 stable releases and official installation/user documentation support ongoing distribution.

review.product_identity: Ceph, the distributed object, block, and file storage system in the core ceph/ceph source repository
review.agency: U.S. Department of Energy/NNSA Advanced Simulation and Computing program through Lawrence Livermore, Los Alamos, and Sandia National Laboratories; research developed at the University of California, Santa Cruz
review.geography: United States (UC Santa Cruz and DOE/NNSA national laboratories)
review.license: Core Ceph source is mostly LGPL-2.1 or LGPL-3.0; see COPYING for file-specific GPL, BSD-style, public-domain, and documentation exceptions
review.status_note: Ceph's official history distinguishes code written in 2004, the project going public under LGPL in 2006, later DreamHost commercialization, and current community governance. The repository URL supplied to SILL is only an organization page; this review maps to the canonical core product repository. Current Ceph is not uniformly LGPL-2.1-only: COPYING lists file-specific grants and exceptions, and the README says most core code is LGPL 2.1 or 3.0. No exact catalog match found.

government_provenance.note: The first-party CFPB repository README says it automates CFPB's Open Source Checklist for release of internal source code; CFPB's official source-code policy describes the Bureau's public-source release process.

public_source.note: The archived public repository contains the scrub.sh utility, Node dependencies, installation and usage instructions, and checklist material.

eligible_license.note: The exact root LICENSE contains the CC0 1.0 Universal dedication. The functional scrub script was added in commit c7b4ef1 on 2016-06-10; the CC0 license file is present from the initial project commit aa03ded on the same date.

primary_evidence.note: The README documents intended internal use and how to run the script, but GitHub marks the repository archived on 2019-02-02, shows no tagged releases, and no current product-specific use or independent adoption was located.

primary_evidence.note: UNICEF’s 2021 ICT Division annual report documents AEDES as a selected-city pathfinding pilot and the 2022 Philippines report describes its dengue prototype; however, the exact current operational use of this repository and maintenance/distribution after its January 2023 last visible source commit are not established.

review.decision_reason: LPG Management is a documented administration UI within the larger Learning Platform Gateway/Civil Service Learning system; its README lists several separate services and deployment dependencies. The repo is public with a full Crown-copyright MIT grant and setup/deploy guidance. Current Cabinet Office guidance confirms Civil Service Learning remains a service, but a 2024 government announcement said Pearson would deliver a new platform; no official source reviewed proves this older LPG repository is the current product code or identifies the independently catalogable family boundary.

government_provenance.note: The exact repository’s full MIT notice identifies Crown Copyright; its README names LPG Management, user/admin tasks and dependencies on the Civil Service Learning services. The current Civil Service Learning privacy notice identifies Cabinet Office responsibility for the learning service.

public_source.note: The public default branch contains the Express/GOV.UK Frontend administration application, build/run/test instructions, Docker packaging and Terraform/Jenkins deployment references.

eligible_license.note: The exact default branch carries the complete OSI-approved MIT grant with Crown Copyright attribution.

primary_evidence.note: The official 2026 privacy notice confirms the current Civil Service Learning service, while the 2024 GOV.UK Pearson procurement announcement signals a replacement platform. Neither page establishes that this older LPG Management code is the current implementation or that it is an independent product; source-to-service parity is unresolved.

review.decision_reason: This is the Companies House web frontend for the exact service “Tell Companies House you have verified someone’s identity.” Its README uses that exact service purpose, and the official GDS beta assessment names Companies House as provider, documents this service for ACSP agents, reports private-beta user completions and frequent real deployments, and rates operation/source-code openness green. Current Companies House ACSP guidance describes how agents use the verification workflow. The first 2024 commit contains both substantive frontend application/validation source and a full Companies House MIT grant. This qualifies as one user-facing service product; the sibling `acsp-api` is a backend microservice and should not be counted as a separate catalog product without family-level justification.

government_provenance.note: The official GDS beta report names Companies House as provider of the exact “Tell Companies House you have verified someone’s identity” service; the repository README describes its frontend as that exact service. The repo is in Companies House’s official source organization.

public_source.note: The public TypeScript/Express frontend source, tests, local setup, form validation and service-specific screens are accessible without credentials.

eligible_license.note: The initial commit on 2024-06-10 includes a full OSI-approved MIT license naming Companies House and the service-specific app source, including the application entry point and identity-verification form validators.

primary_evidence.note: The official beta assessment covers this exact service and reports private-beta completion analytics, real working software, frequent deployments and a green service-operation assessment. Current Companies House ACSP guidance gives users the verification process and follow-up steps; repo README names the same frontend service.

review.decision_reason: The whole core CARE web application is now verified as a two-repository family: the MIT-licensed backend and the separate MIT-licensed care_fe frontend. Their first public grant-bearing commits are March 17 and April 8, 2020 respectively; both canonical repos remain active, and 10BedICU's public organization maintains current forks of both while its current product page identifies CARE as the deployed EMR. AICTE/GDC public support is attributed only to named oxygen-monitoring and critical-care modules, not all CARE code.

government_provenance.note: Government of India's DARPG proceedings describe the CoronaSafe system operating Kerala COVID warrooms and the AICTE/Pupilfirst Global Digital Corps program that built software for National Health Mission warrooms during the oxygen crisis. CARE's own product requirements at https://docs.coronasafe.network/coronasafe-care-documentation specifically say the AICTE-supported fellowship graduates built its real-time oxygen-monitoring and critical-care modules. This establishes product-specific public-agency-supported development, not merely later government use; ACT grants were philanthropic, and the government contribution is attributed specifically to AICTE.

public_source.note: The assigned coronasafe/care URL redirects to canonical ohcnetwork/care. The complete core web app also requires the separate public ohcnetwork/care_fe frontend, whose README links the backend documentation and provides local frontend setup/staging details. GitHub's repository API identifies https://api.github.com/repos/10bedicu/care as a fork whose parent is ohcnetwork/care, and https://api.github.com/repos/10bedicu/care_fe as a fork whose parent is ohcnetwork/care_fe; both were pushed 2026-09-28. This directly maps the current 10BedICU source family to both canonical repos. Optional plugins and deployment infrastructure are outside this core-app scope.

eligible_license.note: I inspected the root grants separately: MIT applies to first-party backend code in ohcnetwork/care, and MIT applies to first-party web-frontend code in ohcnetwork/care_fe (https://github.com/ohcnetwork/care_fe/blob/develop/LICENSE). The backend's first LICENSE-bearing source commit is 2020-03-17; the frontend's is 2020-04-08. These separate grants do not cover optional plug-in repositories, third-party dependencies, or the wider TeleICU/equipment infrastructure.

primary_evidence.note: 10BedICU's current CARE platform page describes CARE as its deployed EMR and documents the hospital-facing patient-management platform and training. GitHub's direct repository API records show https://api.github.com/repos/10bedicu/care is a current fork of ohcnetwork/care and https://api.github.com/repos/10bedicu/care_fe is a current fork of ohcnetwork/care_fe (both pushed 2026-09-28), explicitly mapping the deployed CARE source family to the two canonical repos rather than inferring correspondence from matching names. Meghalaya's government launch record and the 10BedICU program page establish state-government deployment/use; this is not used as proof of authorship.

review.product_identity: CARE core EMR web application: the Coronasafe-origin healthcare patient-management and critical-care platform comprising the CARE backend/API plus the separate care_fe web interface; optional plugins and TeleICU infrastructure are excluded
review.agency: All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE), Government of India, supported the GDC fellowship whose fellows built CARE modules; current product stewardship is with Open Healthcare Network/eGovernments Foundation, with 10BedICU state-government deployments
review.geography: India; originated in Kerala and currently deployed through public-private state programs across multiple states
review.license: MIT for first-party backend source in ohcnetwork/care and separately MIT for first-party web frontend source in ohcnetwork/care_fe; dependencies and optional plugins remain separately licensed
review.family_note: The assigned coronasafe/care path redirects to canonical ohcnetwork/care; the deployed core application is explicitly mapped to the two-repository family by current 10BedICU forks whose GitHub API parent fields point to ohcnetwork/care and ohcnetwork/care_fe. Each repo has its own root MIT grant: backend grant/source commit 2020-03-17 (https://github.com/ohcnetwork/care/commit/9be04171f9a31f82ce038d8c7ed2be2fc9b82998), frontend grant commit 2020-04-08 (https://github.com/ohcnetwork/care_fe/commit/f86d0ee7bb55b5283b939b48503fd51562554cc6). This entry is only the core backend+web-frontend application, not optional ABDM/HMIS/other plugs, TeleICU network infrastructure, or equipment. No catalog match was found.
review.status_note: The core app's first licensed source is dated 2020-03-17 in the backend; the separate frontend's MIT grant was committed 2020-04-08. review.decision_reason: Corosync is a mature, actively maintained open-source cluster engine with a precise BSD grant and independent distribution, but the project history identifies it as a community derivative of OpenAIS developed by private-sector contributors, not a government-created, commissioned, funded, or stewarded product. Its appearance in France's SILL is a discovery/catalog lead and does not establish public provenance.

government_provenance.note: The project's own history says Corosync was created as a derivative of OpenAIS to form a distinct cluster-infrastructure community; the repository's copyright history identifies MontaVista and Red Hat contributors. No public agency authorship, funding, commissioning, or stewardship for this exact product was found. The assigned French SILL listing is not provenance evidence.

public_source.note: The canonical public repository exposes Corosync's complete cluster-engine source, build/install material, documentation, and current source history without credentials.

eligible_license.note: The root license explicitly applies the three-condition BSD grant to every file in the source distribution except git-version-gen and gitlog-to-changelog; those two release-process helpers are GPLv3-or-later and are not part of the generated binary. The scoped BSD-3-Clause grant covers the cluster-engine product code.

primary_evidence.note: Fedora's official package page distributes Corosync as a current cluster-engine package (3.1.10 in the current package metadata) with Fedora build and source links. This is evidence of independent distribution and product maturity, not evidence of government sponsorship or government deployment.

review.product_identity: Corosync Cluster Engine, the OpenAIS-derived cluster messaging, membership, quorum, and service-infrastructure engine
review.agency: No government agency identified; early source history names MontaVista Software and Red Hat contributors, followed by the Corosync developer community
review.geography: International open-source infrastructure project; no government sponsor geography established
review.license: BSD-3-Clause for the Corosync product files; GPL-3.0-or-later for two release-process helper scripts only
review.family_note: Review covers the Corosync Cluster Engine source, not a vendor's HA distribution or any government's use of it. The source history contains earlier OpenAIS code; 2008 is the Corosync product's founding/public project year, not the inherited OpenAIS code's earlier license date. No catalog match was found.
review.status_note: The 2008 Ottawa Linux Symposium paper by project developers describes Corosync as an open-source cluster engine and says it was founded in January 2008; current repository activity reached 2026-09-07. Fedora independently packages the engine. The SILL entry is retained only as the assigned lead and did not affect the provenance decision.

review.decision_reason: Creative Commons Legal Tools is an active public-interest application maintained by Creative Commons, an independent nonprofit, but no government agency authorship, commissioning, funding, or stewardship for this exact application was established. The DPG profile's statement that government institutions use Creative Commons tools is self-reported and does not demonstrate a government's relationship to this source repository.

government_provenance.note: Creative Commons identifies itself as an independent nonprofit organization, and the application README says it is the CC team's tool for managing Creative Commons licenses and public-domain tools. No government agency relationship for this software was found. Use of Creative Commons licenses by public institutions would not prove government origin of this application.

public_source.note: The application repository is public, contains the application source and developer setup, and explicitly links its companion cc-legal-tools-data repository from which it consumes and generates legal-tool data.

eligible_license.note: The assigned application-code repository grants MIT to its first-party software. The companion data repository is a separate content scope with CC0/public-domain and CC-BY-4.0 material as documented in the DPG record; those content grants are not substituted for the app's code license or assumed to relicense dependencies.

primary_evidence.note: The Creative Commons chooser is publicly accessible and the application documentation describes a mature tool managing hundreds of license and public-domain instruments. The DPG record claims broad government/ministerial adoption but labels adopter information self-reported; I found no independent primary source documenting a specific government's use of this application or government distribution of this code. Use of CC legal licenses is not evidence of use of this distinct software.

review.family_note: The application repository is only the executable/data-management part of a two-repository legal-tools suite; this review does not treat CC's license texts or public-domain instruments as source code. review.decision_reason: CREDEBL is a real, actively maintained decentralized-identity platform used as a protocol layer in Bhutan's government National Digital Identity, but the project's first-party sources identify AYANWORKS as its private developer and product owner. Neither deployment of the vendor's platform nor its Digital Public Goods registration establishes government authorship, commissioning, funding, or stewardship of the product source.

government_provenance.note: CREDEBL's own site says the platform was created from AYANWORKS's private team's experience deploying prior identity solutions; the Linux Foundation Decentralized Trust source identifies it as developed and maintained by AYANWORKS. Bhutan's NDI uses CREDEBL as a protocol layer, but that is third-party government use, not proof that the Government of Bhutan funded or created this general product.

public_source.note: The assigned organization is public and links the platform, Studio UI, agent controller, installation tooling, mobile SDK, and reference wallet repositories. The core code is accessible without credentials; the DPG source record points to this organization-level index rather than a single repository.

eligible_license.note: First-party LICENSE files in the core platform, Studio, agent-controller, install, mobile-sdk, platform-admin, webauthn-server, and reference mobile-wallet repositories grant Apache-2.0 to their respective repository code. This is a multi-repository scope, not a grant to every repository or upstream dependency in the AYANWORKS account.

primary_evidence.note: The Royal Government of Bhutan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs reports 2026 integration of the Bhutan NDI wallet/eKYC with the national passport system. CREDEBL's own current technology page says it is the NDI initiative's protocol layer. Together these primary sources verify an operational government use of this exact third-party platform, but not public authorship or funding.

review.product_identity: CREDEBL, AYANWORKS's multi-repository self-sovereign/decentralized identity and verifiable-credential platform, including the platform service, Studio UI, agent controller, installation tools, SDK, and reference wallet
review.agency: No government creator or source sponsor identified; private product owner/developer AYANWORKS; Royal Government of Bhutan is a documented downstream user of CREDEBL within NDI
review.geography: Developed by AYANWORKS in India; deployed as the protocol layer for Bhutan's national digital identity
review.license: Apache-2.0 for the identified first-party CREDEBL core repositories, with per-repository scopes; dependencies and any non-core or upstream code remain separately licensed
review.family_note: The assigned URL is an organization page. The reviewed product is the identified CREDEBL suite, not every AYANWORKS repository; core components and license scopes are named separately. Government NDI deployment is treated as third-party use only. No catalog match was found.
review.status_note: The earliest inspected first-party CREDEBL UI source with an Apache grant dates from 2023-06-21; the core platform repository began in 2023-08. The platform source remains active, with code updates in September 2026, and current product/docs pages link to the platform. Current Bhutan government use is corroborated by the Royal Government's 2026 NDI service announcement plus CREDEBL's explicit implementation mapping. No exact catalog match was found.

public_source.note: The organization page is public and its README describes Dalgo and links code, but it is not a canonical repository. eligible_license.note: The organization README states Dalgo is AGPL-3.0 and the DPGA marks the product-level AGPL-3.0 license as verified; the public DDP_backend repo also has an AGPL-3.0 root grant. Do not apply one repository's text automatically to the complete family.

primary_evidence.note: Project Tech4Dev's product launch page identifies Dalgo v1.0 as its open-source data platform and records pilots/early adopters including Dost Education, SNEHA, STiR Education, SHRI and Antarang. review.agency: No government product sponsor identified; privately owned/developed by Project Tech4Dev. State Governments are mentioned as downstream NGO-partner environments only.

review.status_note: Project Tech4Dev announced Dalgo v1.0 as open source in September 2023 and describes Dalgo 2.0 as its evolving social-sector platform. That launch date is not used as a first public licensed-source year because the assigned org URL does not identify a single canonical repo or a family-wide first grant commit. The exact repository documents its product role, setup and production build; its actual MIT grant expressly excludes Marianne font and public-directory illustrations/images. First explicit source-code license is 2025.

public_source.note: The active public source includes application files, setup and build instructions, production deployment pointers, and current commit activity.

eligible_license.note: The actual MIT grant was added with the license file on 2025-07-03: https://github.com/datagouv/cdata/commit/b9159f301a55cc4fbb5da6c4b790df08fbd42640. It explicitly excludes the Marianne font and images in public; README further warns that government identity elements and private illustrations/images are not licensed for reuse. Keep the claim scoped to the rest of repo code.

primary_evidence.note: The exact product README identifies cdata as the data.gouv.fr frontend and gives prerequisites, setup, local development, production build, and Docker run instructions. The official platform legal notice names DINUM as publisher: https://www.data.gouv.fr/pages/legal/legal-notice.

primary_evidence.note: DataKind's 2025 product-specific article says DOT is already making a difference in Uganda and Lesotho; the project repository supplies runnable Docker setup and UI/user guidance, and Medic's Uganda reports document MoH training/deployment work. review.decision_reason: Decidim is an operational, installable participatory-democracy platform/framework published by the Barcelona City Council and documented for deployment. The Spanish CTT identifies the exact product, responsible city authority, AGPLv3, and production status; an official 2017 Barcelona report documents independent adoption by 12 municipalities and institutions. The source is public and the root code grant is AGPLv3.

government_provenance.note: Spain’s public-administration CTT entry names Decidim, Ayuntamiento de Barcelona as responsible, AGPL v3, and production status. Barcelona’s own 2017 press page says the City promoted the platform and other municipalities/institutions were building platforms from it: https://ajuntament.barcelona.cat/premsa/2017/10/23/lajuntament-de-barcelona-exporta-el-decidim-a-12-municipis-i-institucions/.

public_source.note: The public canonical repository contains the Ruby on Rails application/framework, multiple gems, install/development documentation, and release history. The repository README describes the Barcelona origin; the CTT page links to project source resources.

eligible_license.note: The dated 2016-10-14 license-history commit moves the project license to GNU AGPL v3; the current root LICENSE-AGPLv3.txt is the standard AGPL version 3 text. This supports the code repository only; platform content and participatory-process data have separate terms and are not included in the license claim.

primary_evidence.note: The exact CTT record describes the citizen-participation platform, identifies Barcelona as responsible, and reports production status. The City of Barcelona reports 12 municipalities/institutions using or developing from Decidim in 2017, satisfying documented independent reuse: https://ajuntament.barcelona.cat/premsa/2017/10/23/lajuntament-de-barcelona-exporta-el-decidim-a-12-municipis-i-institucions/.

review.product_identity: Decidim, the Barcelona-origin participatory-democracy platform and reusable Ruby on Rails framework for citizen participation processes
review.agency: Ajuntament de Barcelona (Barcelona City Council)
review.license: AGPL-3.0 (repository code; process content/data have separate terms)
review.family_note: This is the Decidim platform/framework, distinct from the older Consul software that informed the initial Barcelona project. The source repository is a multi-gem codebase; do not treat user-generated content, hosted participation data, or third-party dependencies as covered by the root AGPL grant.
review.status_note: The official documentation describes Decidim Barcelona as presented in February 2016, while the cited license-history commit dated 2016-10-14 explicitly moved the source to AGPL v3. The latter is used as the first defensible public eligible-code date. Documentation is available at https://docs.decidim.org/; the official Barcelona live participation portal is https://www.decidim.barcelona/.

review.decision_reason: The Department for Education's live Register trainee teachers service and provider guidance establish an operational national service; the repository README identifies the service and production domain. The public code carries MIT terms, first evidenced in 2020.

government_provenance.note: DfE's official guidance identifies the Register trainee teachers service and its use by teacher-training providers in England.

public_source.note: The public repository contains the service source; its README names DfE and the production register-trainee-teachers.service.gov.uk service.

eligible_license.note: The repository LICENCE grants MIT terms; the initial licensed application commit is dated 2020-08-13 (https://github.com/DFE-Digital/register-trainee-teachers/commit/5727e3ca1a22195be31c13c996d5c95129ceb0ca).

primary_evidence.note: DfE documentation says the service replaced the Database of Trainee Teachers and is used to register trainees, record outcomes and check funding.

review.decision_reason: DFIR ORC is ANSSI-developed and ANSSI-managed forensic collection software for Windows incident response. The main repository has public build and configuration documentation, versioned releases, and is identified by ANSSI as used by its operational teams. This decision is for the core orchestrator repository, not every separately licensed tool or configuration in the broader release family.

government_provenance.note: The repository README says the project is managed by ANSSI. ANSSI describes DFIR ORC in its official project directory as a set of tools used in particular by its Operations subdirectorate during cyber-incident response: https://anssi-fr.github.io/README.en.html.

public_source.note: The public repository contains the C++ core source, build scripts, instructions, and release history. The assigned URL resolves to the canonical DFIR-ORC organization repository.

eligible_license.note: The README explicitly grants LGPL 2.1+ for contents of this repository and the checked-in license text is the LGPL v2.1 text. Record LGPL-2.1-or-later for this core repo only. ANSSI marks its name/logo and separately published tools/configuration as outside this repository license scope.

primary_evidence.note: ANSSI states its DFIR-ORC tool set is used by the agency CERT in incident investigations. The official project documentation explains artifact collection, build requirements, configuration and tutorial guidance, and that the broader release includes separate repositories for the main program, filesystem tools, collection tools, and configurations.

review.agency: Agence nationale de la sécurité des systèmes d’information (ANSSI)
review.license: LGPL-2.1-or-later (core repository; excludes ANSSI marks and separately published components)

Official docs say a usable release also involves separate filesystem-tool, collection-tool, and configuration repositories; this row does not transfer the core repo license to those components or treat them as independent products.
review.status_note: The initial public commit contains only a README stub; the first license-bearing source release is the 2019-09-23 v10.0.0 commit cited above. The repository README expressly says LGPL 2.1+ although the bundled license text is the v2.1 text. The tool was developed earlier for ANSSI operational needs, but first defensible licensed-source year is 2019.

review.decision_reason: Ketu is a complete, public MIT-licensed K2 transit-search pipeline and the peer-reviewed paper using the exact code documents a scientific use that produced 36 planet candidates. The paper acknowledges partial NASA grant support for several authors, but it does not identify that award as funding for Ketu development, and I found no separate NASA release, commissioning, or stewardship record for this repository. Hold until a project-level NASA relationship is established; the NASA mission data and catalog lead do not by themselves prove a government relationship.

government_provenance.note: The paper links the exact dfm/ketu implementation and acknowledges that three authors were partially supported by NASA grant NNX12AI50G, but it does not state that the grant funded development of this code. No NASA commissioning or stewardship evidence was found.

public_source.note: The public repository exposes the pipeline implementation and accompanying documentation without credentials.

eligible_license.note: The repository's MIT license is independently identified by the peer-reviewed paper, which explicitly says the linked implementation is released under the MIT open-source software license.

primary_evidence.note: The peer-reviewed paper uses and links this exact pipeline, documents the resulting candidate search, and acknowledges NASA grant support; it is primary scholarly evidence of product identity and use.

review.decision_reason: The assigned repository is the public SistemaUnicoSCU codebase from Italy's Department for Youth Policies and Universal Civil Service (PCM-DGSCU), including the Helios/Futuro workflows and the DOL online application. The official Developers Italia record names the department as publisher and manager and links this exact repository as source; the live official DOL service is taking applications under a current 2026 call and provides applicant instructions. The first public source code appeared in 2022 under GPL-3.0; the repository's current first-party grant is AGPL-3.0-only. The repository metadata lists mandatory third-party dependencies, including proprietary products, which are not covered by the repository grant. No catalog entry was added.

government_provenance.note: The official DTD/AgID Developers Italia record identifies the Dipartimento per le politiche giovanili e il Servizio civile universale (PCM) as publisher and PCM-DGSCU as manager, links this exact repository as source, and describes the application as prepared by the department with the Servizio civile system. The repository README identifies itself as DGSCU's Sistema Unico SCU.

public_source.note: The assigned repository is public and contains application code, database scripts, web services, the DOL application, and user manuals without credentials.

eligible_license.note: The current root LICENSE contains the full GNU Affero GPL version 3 grant (AGPL-3.0-only) for first-party repository code. The root license began as GPL-3.0 in 2022 and was changed to AGPL-3.0 in 2024. The repository's publiccode.yml separately lists mandatory third-party dependencies including Aspose.PDF, Aspose.Words, Microsoft SQL Server, CrystalReports, and Ionic.Zip; those components are not covered by this source grant.

primary_evidence.note: The official citizen-facing service is live and currently advertises a 2026 call for 3,767 volunteer positions, with SPID/CIE access instructions. The official software record marks SistemaUnicoSCU stable and used by the department, and the exact repository contains versioned user manuals and technical documentation.

review.product_identity: SistemaUnicoSCU, the department's web application suite for the Italian Universal Civil Service, comprising Helios/Futuro workflows and the Domanda On Line (DOL) applicant service
review.agency: Dipartimento per le politiche giovanili e il Servizio civile universale (PCM-DGSCU), Presidency of the Council of Ministers, Italy
review.license: AGPL-3.0-only for current first-party source in the repository; the initial 2022 code commit followed a root GPL-3.0 grant. Required third-party proprietary dependencies listed in publiccode.yml are outside this grant and may impose separate deployment terms.
review.family_note: The repository is one suite containing SistemaUnicoSCU workflows and DOL, not a standalone authentication library. Manuals are under Manuali Utente. The root AGPL grant is scoped to repository first-party source, not dependencies named in publiccode.yml; it does not make those proprietary dependencies open source.
review.status_note: The root initial commit on 2022-08-05 contains a full GPL-3.0 license; the first public DOL source commit is 2022-10-21 (linked above). A 2024 commit changed the repository grant to AGPL-3.0. review.decision_reason: This is the Digital Agency’s reusable source implementation for its Name Matching Support Service model, not merely the service’s API sample. The Agency’s developer site names this exact repository as the source-code distribution for the self-hosting option, and explains that the software can be customized and independently deployed. The repository provides a command-line implementation, training/inference code, examples, and MIT terms; the first public MIT source commit is dated 2025-02-13. The service terms generally restrict reproduction/modification of service intellectual property in Article 7(3), but Article 7(4) expressly directs programs/source code with an individually displayed license to follow that license, preserving this repository’s explicit MIT grant. Treat it as a component/product within the Name Matching Support Service family, not a second listing for the hosted API. Separately hosted dictionaries and pretrained weights have their own resource terms and are not assumed to be covered by this source-code license.

government_provenance.note: The official Agency developer page links this exact repository as the source code for the Agency-provided Name Matching Support model and says it supports an independently managed, self-hosted deployment.

public_source.note: The code for matching, inference, training, CLI execution, and sample programs is public without credentials; support-site model weights/dictionary resources are distributed separately.

eligible_license.note: The source repository has a root MIT license naming the Digital Agency; Git history shows the license and initial versioned source commit on 2025-02-13 (https://github.com/digital-go-jp/kanjikana-model/commit/8c21c06137c68f970efdd0fab5ecba66360afc96). The Agency service terms Article 7(4) expressly makes an individual license displayed for software/source control over the general restrictions in Article 7(3) (https://developers.digital.go.jp/documents/name-matching-support/terms-of-use/), so the repository’s explicit MIT source grant remains operative. README identifies external training/dictionary datasets and asks users to follow their own terms; separately hosted model weights/dictionaries are not assumed to be covered by the source repo MIT grant.

primary_evidence.note: The Agency’s service documentation identifies the four API/model functions, provides the model source and model-resource paths, and explicitly describes self-hosting/customization. The repository README states that this CLI model is also used inside the operational Agency service.

review.decision_reason: This repository is the Digital Agency’s named, distributable Python converter for Ministry of Justice registry-map XML to GeoJSON, developed to support the Address Base Registry. The Agency’s January 2023 announcement says it developed and released the converter as open-source software; README provides Python installation, CLI, Docker, and test instructions. The full source is public under an MIT license with Digital Agency copyright, first present in the 2023-01-23 initial source commit. Although the repository’s latest source push is 2023-10-28, the current DDA Address Base Registry page (last updated 2026-03-30) still links this exact repository as the converter and documents ongoing registry work; under the intake baseline this supports a Maintained status, not Active. The Agency says it improved an earlier Ministry of Agriculture converter, so retain that lineage note.

government_provenance.note: The Agency announcement dated 2023-01-23 says the Digital Agency developed and published the Map XML-to-GeoJSON converter as OSS for use with registry-map data and the Address Base Registry; it states the converter was improved from an earlier Ministry of Agriculture converter.

eligible_license.note: The repository provides standard MIT terms naming Digital Agency copyright; the LICENSE and initial source were present in commit af36568ef5e846efa106d0f5f746d5efd679f58b dated 2023-01-23 (https://github.com/digital-go-jp/mojxml2geojson/commit/af36568ef5e846efa106d0f5f746d5efd679f58b).

primary_evidence.note: The current Agency Address Base Registry page was last updated 2026-03-30 and directly links this exact repository under related information as the Ministry of Justice registry-map XML-to-GeoJSON converter. The page documents ongoing registry work; this current product/source link establishes continuing official use and source parity for the stale-source exception. The earlier DDA release announcement (https://www.digital.go.jp/news/4b7250a3-3fcf-4b83-8d52-4bb131e1ba9d) establishes initial publication, tool behavior, and user context.

government_provenance.note: The official DISIC GitHub organization identifies itself as DINUM (Direction Interministérielle du Numérique), links numerique.gouv.fr, and owns the assigned policy repository.

public_source.note: The repository contains policy prose, FAQ/governance and guidance documents, and lists of public organizations/repositories; it does not publish source code for a software product.

eligible_license.note: The README says the policy document is published under Licence Ouverte 2.0. That statement scopes to the document/content, not software source in a product; no qualifying code grant is present for this review.

primary_evidence.note: The repository describes itself as a policy for opening government source code and says its content is being archived/reintegrated into guides; GitHub marks it archived/read-only since Nov. 10, 2021. It is not an independently notable software product.

primary_evidence.note: The official 2026 national report page directs readers to the complete assessment on SDGital2030.ch; the 2021 FDFA source identifies the federal reporting tool.

review.decision_reason: The exact API component is a public Apache-2.0 repository within ESUP-OTP, a university MFA system, but it is not independently notable as a product. Product-level licensing and deployments require review of the manager, CAS integration, and mobile application repositories.

government_provenance.note: The official ESUP-Portail project page names the ESUP-OTP system, participating public universities (Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne, La Rochelle, Rouen), the exact esup-otp-api repository, and describes it as the business/API component calculating tokens and secrets.

public_source.note: The component source is publicly accessible and includes README/setup information and the source license.

eligible_license.note: The actual repository license is Apache-2.0; the license file was added in the 2016-03-17 commit https://github.com/EsupPortail/esup-otp-api/commit/1158b3c5420dc97b237c1a767fd6d8732e3ec7d0. This claim covers this API repository only, not linked manager, CAS, or mobile-app components.

primary_evidence.note: The official docs establish this API as part of the deployable ESUP-OTP suite, but the suite also comprises separate manager, CAS plugin, CAS server, and mobile-app repositories. This API alone is a backend component; independently notable deployment/use and complete material-component license scope have not been shown.

review.product_identity: esup-otp-api, backend API component of the multi-repository ESUP-OTP multi-factor-authentication solution
review.agency: ESUP-Portail consortium and participating public universities: Université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne, La Rochelle Université, and Université de Rouen Normandie
review.license: Apache-2.0 (API repository only)
review.family_note: Do not infer suite-wide license from this repository. The official project lists distinct `esup-otp-manager`, `esup-otp-cas`, `esup-otp-cas-server`, and `esup-otp-push` repositories; review them before deciding a whole-suite entry.
review.status_note: Clear the hold by deciding whether the catalog identity can be the API backend alone with independently documented use, or by reviewing all material ESUP-OTP repositories and assigning a family-level license. The current decision does not deny the utility of the complete university MFA suite.

primary_evidence.note: Official deployment list names Ministry of Education/DNE PodÉduc (809,843 staff) and many production university, ministry, and institute instances. Project docs link installation/configuration guidance.

review.decision_reason: OpenGateLLM is an actively maintained MIT-licensed gateway developed and maintained by DINUM, deployed as the core of Albert API, and officially offered for public-administration deployment with technical documentation and a self-hosting path.

government_provenance.note: The official IA dans l’État page explicitly identifies Albert API as the DINUM instance of OpenGateLLM and says OpenGateLLM is open-source software developed by the French State; its deployment page states DINUM maintains OpenGateLLM.

public_source.note: The public repository contains Python gateway source, actual MIT license, a current quickstart and deployment documentation, and release history.

eligible_license.note: The actual MIT grant was added on 2024-07-16 in https://github.com/etalab-ia/OpenGateLLM/commit/f2aee94e06027229292160674524d285d88812d2. Repository root history with earlier imported dates is not used to date public licensed product source; first defensible licensed-source year is 2024. Model weights and external API provider materials keep their own licenses.

primary_evidence.note: The official deployment page calls OpenGateLLM the open-source solution behind Albert API, says DINUM maintains it with an active community, and offers administration deployment support. The exact README documents quickstart and self-hosting.

review.product_identity: OpenGateLLM, an open-source gateway for administering, routing, and securing access to generative-AI model APIs; deployed by DINUM as Albert API
review.agency: Direction interministérielle du numérique (DINUM), Etalab/IA dans l’État
review.license: MIT
review.family_note: OpenGateLLM is the software gateway and Albert API its DINUM-operated deployment; avoid counting the government instance as a second software product. Models and provider services connected through the gateway are not covered by the MIT grant.
review.status_note: The repository’s initial 2024-06 history was imported before GitHub repo creation and begins with README-only material; use the actual MIT LICENSE addition on 2024-07-16 as the first defensible public licensed-source evidence. Official pages identify the exact source-to-Albert relationship and DINUM maintenance.

review.decision_reason: Geonovum publishes a working OGC/JSON-FG validation tool as a live web app and versioned npm CLI with user installation guidance. government_provenance.note: Geonovum's official page identifies it as an overheidsstichting; the exact repository's publiccode.yml names Geonovum as main copyright owner and the tool is published under the Geonovum GitHub organization.

public_source.note: The exact public repository contains the TypeScript checker application, tests, build configuration, README and license. No credentials are required.

eligible_license.note: Inspected the actual EUPL-1.2 text. The directly inspected functional-source snapshot is the 2026-03-05 switch commit https://github.com/Geonovum/ogc-checker/commit/beccec478ea10f2d22276b846afa52e8aa7e9700, where src/main.ts and the EUPL grant coexist. The 2023 initial snapshot was README/LICENSE-only; it is not used to date functional source.

primary_evidence.note: Geonovum maintains the exact checker as a live browser application; its README documents npm/npx installation and use. The package registry reports version 1.3.1 under EUPL-1.2, published 2026-09-09: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@geonovum/ogc-checker.

review.decision_reason: This is a separately installable Geonovum validation framework, distributed as a versioned npm package with installation and integration documentation. Its README identifies two distinct checker applications built on it (OGC Checker and DON Checker), demonstrating actual reuse beyond an internal module. Functional source and an eligible grant are public.

government_provenance.note: Geonovum's official page identifies it as an overheidsstichting. The exact repository publiccode.yml names Geonovum as main copyright owner, and the package is published by the Geonovum GitHub organization.

public_source.note: Public TypeScript source, test/build setup, integration README, publiccode.yml and license are available without credentials.

eligible_license.note: Current root LICENSE is actual EUPL-1.2 text. The earliest directly inspected functional licensed snapshot is commit https://github.com/Geonovum/standards-checker/commit/abc46c7a0be29799beffd66f78e199f09b575de7 (2025-10-21): it contains functional src/index.ts and an explicit MIT grant; this was later changed to EUPL-1.2 at https://github.com/Geonovum/standards-checker/commit/00fde8ed1eea687f67a4a5cdd72ac3fa36a62b24. Both grants are eligible.

primary_evidence.note: The project README documents a reusable CLI, programmatic engine, embeddable UI, installation/integration steps, release process, and identifies OGC Checker and DON Checker as consumer applications. The current npm package is version 1.4.0, EUPL-1.2, published 2026-09-09: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@geonovum/standards-checker.

review.product_identity: @geonovum/standards-checker reusable validation framework (CLI toolkit, API, React UI and shared tooling)
review.agency: Stichting Geonovum
review.license: MIT (first inspected functional-source snapshot); current EUPL-1.2
review.family_note: Shared framework, distinct from consuming OGC Checker and DON Checker applications; README names both, and the framework has its own package, release stream and installation documentation.
review.status_note: Historical grant changed from MIT to EUPL-1.2; both are eligible. First directly inspected snapshot combining executable framework source and explicit grant is 2025-10-21.
